title: NICE NG122 Lung cancer: diagnosis and management, 1.1 Information and support
sections: Information and support
NICE NG122 recommendation 1.1.1 says a lung cancer clinical nurse specialist should be available to people with lung cancer at every stage of their care.

title: NICE NG122 Lung cancer: diagnosis and management, 1.2 Diagnosis and staging
sections: Diagnosis and staging

NICE NG122 recommends contrast enhanced CT of the chest that also covers the liver, adrenal glands and lower neck for people with suspected lung cancer, and advises caution with contrast in renal impairment (recommendation 1.2.2). PET-CT should be offered before treatment with curative intent, and cancer alliances should provide rapid access to it (recommendations 1.2.4 and 1.2.5). MRI is not used routinely for T staging, but may be used for superior sulcus tumours (recommendations 1.2.6 and 1.2.7). EBUS guided transbronchial needle aspiration is offered for paratracheal and peribronchial lesions, and each cancer alliance should have at least one EBUS or EUS centre with audited test performance (recommendations 1.2.8 to 1.2.10). Samples should be adequate for diagnosis, histological subtyping and molecular markers, and next generation sequencing panels should follow the National Genomic Test Directory (recommendations 1.2.11 and 1.2.12). For mediastinal lymph nodes under 10 mm in short axis PET-CT is the preferred first test; for nodes of 10 mm or more PET-CT is followed by EBUS guided TBNA and/or EUS guided FNA, and surgical mediastinal staging is considered when EBUS or EUS is negative but suspicion remains high and the result would change treatment (recommendations 1.2.19 to 1.2.22). Brain imaging depends on stage: no dedicated brain imaging for asymptomatic clinical stage 1 disease, contrast enhanced CT of the head for stage 2 disease with MRI if suspicious, and contrast enhanced MRI of the head for stage 3 disease (recommendations 1.2.24 to 1.2.26). People with suspected lung cancer should be referred to a lung cancer multidisciplinary team and all working diagnoses discussed at MDT meetings (recommendations 1.2.31 and 1.2.32).

title: NICE NG122 Lung cancer: diagnosis and management, 1.3 Stop smoking interventions
sections: Stop smoking interventions

NG122 advises telling people that smoking increases the risk of pulmonary complications after lung cancer surgery and advising them to stop as soon as lung cancer is suspected (recommendations 1.3.1 and 1.3.2). Surgery should not be delayed to allow a person to stop smoking (recommendation 1.3.3).

title: NICE NG122 Lung cancer: diagnosis and management, 1.4 Assessing people with NSCLC for treatment with curative intent
sections: Assessing people with NSCLC for treatment with curative intent

NG122 suggests considering a global risk score such as Thoracoscore when estimating the risk of death from surgery, and making sure the person understands that risk before consenting (recommendation 1.4.1). Lung resection should be avoided within 30 days of a myocardial infarction, and people with an active cardiac condition, three or more cardiac risk factors or poor cardiorespiratory function should be referred for cardiology review (recommendations 1.4.2 to 1.4.8). Spirometry and transfer factor (TLCO) are measured in everyone considered for curative treatment, predicted postoperative lung function is calculated with a functional segment count, and treatment with curative intent can still be offered when predicted postoperative FEV1 or TLCO is below 30% if the person accepts the higher risk of dyspnoea and complications (recommendations 1.4.9 to 1.4.14). A shuttle walk test distance above 400 m or cardiopulmonary exercise testing with VO2 max above 15 ml/kg/min can be used to assess fitness for surgery in people at moderate to high risk of postoperative dyspnoea (recommendation 1.4.14).

title: NICE NG122 Lung cancer: diagnosis and management, 1.5 Surgery and radiotherapy with curative intent for NSCLC
sections: Surgery and radiotherapy with curative intent for NSCLC

NG122 recommends lobectomy, by an open or thoracoscopic approach, for people with NSCLC who are well enough and for whom treatment with curative intent is suitable (recommendation 1.5.1). For stage 1 to 2a (T1a to T2b, N0, M0) NSCLC in people who decline lobectomy or for whom it is unsuitable, SABR or sublobar resection is offered (recommendation 1.5.5). For stage 1 to 2a NSCLC when surgery is declined or unsuitable, SABR is offered; if SABR is contraindicated, conventional or hyperfractionated radiotherapy is offered (recommendation 1.5.8). For stage 3a or 3b disease in people who cannot tolerate or decline chemoradiotherapy, radical radiotherapy can be considered (recommendations 1.5.9 and 1.5.10). For conventionally fractionated radical radiotherapy NG122 lists 55 Gy in 20 fractions over 4 weeks, or 60 Gy to 66 Gy in 30 to 33 fractions over 6 to 6.5 weeks, and SABR fractionation follows the UK SABR Consortium guidance (recommendations 1.5.11 and 1.5.12).

title: NICE NG122 Lung cancer: diagnosis and management, 1.6 Multimodality treatment for NSCLC
sections: Multimodality treatment for NSCLC

For operable stage 3a N2 NSCLC in people fit for multimodality treatment, NG122 suggests considering chemoradiotherapy followed by surgery, with surgery 3 to 5 weeks after chemoradiotherapy (recommendations 1.6.3 to 1.6.5). Neoadjuvant nivolumab with platinum based chemotherapy is an option for resectable NSCLC (technology appraisal TA876, recommendation 1.6.8). Durvalumab with platinum based chemotherapy before surgery and then durvalumab alone after surgery is an option for resectable NSCLC without EGFR or ALK alterations (technology appraisal TA1030, recommendation 1.6.9). Pembrolizumab with platinum based chemotherapy before surgery and then pembrolizumab alone after surgery is an option for resectable NSCLC at high risk of recurrence (technology appraisal TA1017, recommendation 1.6.10). Postoperative chemotherapy with a platinum based combination is offered to people with WHO performance status 0 or 1 and T1a to T4, N1 to N2, M0 NSCLC, and considered for T2b to T4, N0, M0 tumours larger than 4 cm (recommendations 1.6.11 to 1.6.13). Adjuvant osimertinib is recommended after complete resection of stage 1b to 3a NSCLC with an EGFR exon 19 deletion or exon 21 L858R substitution, with treatment stopped at 3 years (technology appraisal TA1043, recommendation 1.6.14). Adjuvant alectinib is recommended after complete resection of ALK positive stage 1b (tumour at least 4 cm) to 3a NSCLC (technology appraisal TA1014, recommendation 1.6.15). Adjuvant atezolizumab or pembrolizumab may be used in defined high risk groups after resection and adjuvant chemotherapy, as set out in technology appraisals TA1071 and TA1037 (recommendation 1.6.16). Chemoradiotherapy is considered for stage 2 to 3 NSCLC that is unsuitable for surgery, balancing the survival benefit against toxicity (recommendation 1.6.17). Durvalumab is an option for maintenance treatment after platinum based chemoradiation for unresectable NSCLC that has not progressed, when PD-L1 is expressed on at least 1% of tumour cells (technology appraisal TA798, recommendation 1.6.18).

title: NICE NG122 Lung cancer: diagnosis and management, 1.7 Systemic anticancer therapy for advanced and metastatic NSCLC
sections: Systemic anticancer therapy for advanced and metastatic NSCLC

NG122 organises systemic treatment of advanced NSCLC into treatment pathways for squamous and non squamous disease, divided by PD-L1 expression below 50% or at least 50% and by actionable biomarkers: EGFR TK mutations, ALK, ROS1, BRAF V600, MET exon 14 skipping, RET fusions and KRAS G12C. Larotrectinib is available through the Cancer Drugs Fund for NTRK fusion positive solid tumours when there are no satisfactory treatment options (technology appraisal TA630, recommendation 1.7.1). NG122 recommendation 1.7.2 lists medicines that NICE does not recommend for some lung cancer populations, including cemiplimab, amivantamab, pralsetinib, nivolumab with ipilimumab and chemotherapy, necitumumab and ramucirumab, and refers to the individual technology appraisals for the populations concerned.

title: NICE NG122 Lung cancer: diagnosis and management, 1.8-1.12 Small cell lung cancer
sections: Small cell lung cancer

People with small cell lung cancer should see a thoracic oncologist within 1 week of the decision to recommend treatment (recommendation 1.8.1), and surgery can be considered for early stage SCLC (T1 to 2a, N0, M0) (recommendation 1.9.1). For limited stage SCLC NG122 recommends 4 to 6 cycles of cisplatin based combination chemotherapy, with carboplatin considered when renal function is impaired, WHO performance status is 2 or more, or comorbidity is significant (recommendation 1.10.1). For limited stage SCLC in people with WHO performance status 0 or 1, twice daily thoracic radiotherapy is given concurrently with chemotherapy starting in the first or second cycle, with once daily radiotherapy if twice daily is declined or not possible (recommendations 1.10.2 and 1.10.3). Prophylactic cranial irradiation at 25 Gy in 10 fractions is offered to people with limited stage SCLC and WHO performance status 0 to 2 whose disease has not progressed on first line treatment (recommendation 1.10.5). Durvalumab is an option after platinum based chemoradiotherapy for limited stage SCLC that has not progressed (technology appraisal TA1099, recommendation 1.10.6). For extensive stage SCLC, platinum based combination chemotherapy is offered to people fit enough, up to a maximum of 6 cycles, and durvalumab with etoposide and platinum (TA1041) or atezolizumab with carboplatin and etoposide (TA638) are options for people with a WHO or ECOG performance status of 0 or 1 (recommendations 1.11.1 to 1.11.3). For relapsed SCLC, people should be referred to a thoracic oncologist; an anthracycline containing regimen or platinum rechallenge for up to 6 cycles, or oral topotecan (TA184), can be offered when further chemotherapy is suitable (recommendations 1.12.1 to 1.12.4). Tarlatamab is not recommended for SCLC that has progressed after 2 or more lines of treatment including platinum based chemotherapy (technology appraisal TA1091, recommendation 1.12.6).

title: NICE NG122 Lung cancer: diagnosis and management, 1.13-1.15 Palliative interventions and supportive care
sections: Palliative interventions and supportive care

Palliative radiotherapy should be available to people who cannot have curative treatment (recommendation 1.13.1). Large airway involvement should be monitored, and radiotherapy and/or endobronchial debulking or stenting offered for impending airway obstruction, with rapid access to interventional endobronchial treatment (recommendations 1.14.1 to 1.14.3). Symptomatic pleural effusions are aspirated or drained, with talc pleurodesis offered when long term benefit is likely (recommendations 1.15.1 and 1.15.2). For superior vena cava obstruction, chemotherapy and radiotherapy are offered according to stage and performance status, and stent insertion is considered for severe symptoms or when earlier treatment has failed (recommendations 1.15.7 and 1.15.8).

title: NICE NG122 Lung cancer: diagnosis and management, 1.16-1.18 Brain and bone metastases and other symptoms
sections: Brain and bone metastases and other symptoms

Dexamethasone is offered for symptomatic brain metastases at the lowest effective maintenance dose, with management following NICE guideline NG99 on brain tumours and metastases (recommendations 1.16.1 and 1.16.2). Single fraction radiotherapy is offered for bone metastases when pain control is inadequate (recommendation 1.17.1), denosumab is an option to prevent skeletal related events from bone metastases of solid tumours other than prostate when bisphosphonates would otherwise be used (TA265), and spinal metastases are managed according to NICE NG234. Weight loss, loss of appetite, depression, difficulty swallowing and fatigue should be managed by multidisciplinary groups that include supportive and palliative care professionals (recommendation 1.18.1).

title: NICE NG122 Lung cancer: diagnosis and management, 1.19 Follow up
sections: Follow up

After lung cancer treatment, NG122 recommends an initial specialist follow up appointment within 6 weeks of completing treatment, then regular scheduled appointments (recommendation 1.19.1). Protocol driven follow up led by a lung cancer clinical nurse specialist is offered to people with a life expectancy of more than 3 months, and people should know how to contact their nurse specialist between visits (recommendations 1.19.2 and 1.19.3).

title: NICE CG121 Lung cancer: diagnosis and management (2011)
sections: Status

NICE CG121 was the 2011 NICE guideline on the diagnosis and management of lung cancer, covering staging, surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy for NSCLC and SCLC. It was withdrawn and replaced by NG122 in March 2019, so its recommendations should not be used for current practice.

NICE technology appraisal TA428, pembrolizumab for treating pd-l1 positive non small cell lung cancer after chemotherapy, was published on 2017-01-11. This appraisal covers pembrolizumab for locally advanced or metastatic PD-L1 positive NSCLC after at least one chemotherapy regimen.

title: NICE TA798: Durvalumab for maintenance treatment of unresectable non small cell lung cancer after platinum based chemoradiation
sections: Summary

NICE technology appraisal TA798, durvalumab for maintenance treatment of unresectable non small cell lung cancer after platinum based chemoradiation, was published on 2022-06-22. NICE recommends durvalumab as an option for maintenance treatment of locally advanced unresectable NSCLC in adults whose tumours express PD-L1 on at least 1% of tumour cells and whose disease has not progressed after platinum based chemoradiation.

sections: Summary

NICE technology appraisal TA823, atezolizumab for adjuvant treatment of resected non small cell lung cancer, was published on 2022-09-28. This appraisal covers adjuvant atezolizumab after complete resection and platinum based chemotherapy for NSCLC, based on the IMpower010 trial; consult the appraisal for the stage and PD-L1 restrictions. title: NICE TA761: Osimertinib for adjuvant treatment of EGFR mutation positive non small cell lung cancer after complete tumour resection (2022)
sections: Status

NICE TA761, published on 19 January 2022, made adjuvant osimertinib available for completely resected EGFR mutation positive NSCLC through the Cancer Drugs Fund. It has been replaced by TA1043, which recommends adjuvant osimertinib for stage 1b to 3a disease and stops treatment at 3 years.
